question: According to complaints from more than 300 Italian citizens legally resident in Bulgaria, in 2023 Italy unilaterally amended the interpretation of the 1988 Bilateral Convention for the Avoidance of Double Taxation by re-imposing taxation of (private) National Social Security Institute (INPS) pensions in Italy unless the pensioner also holds Bulgarian citizenship.
This clause, contained in Article 1(2) of the convention, is unique in the context of Italian tax treaties and leads to de facto discrimination on a national basis.

It is in breach of Articles 18 (prohibition of discrimination on grounds of nationality), 21 and 45 (freedom of movement and residence) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), as well as the principle of legitimate expectations and legal certainty.
In addition, there are serious economic and social consequences, also confirmed by official documentation and first-instance judgments in favour of the pensioners. In the light of the above: 1.
Will the Commission check that the aforementioned clause in the Italy-Bulgaria convention is compatible with EU law and, if necessary, urge Italy to revise the agreement?
Does it believe that the retroactive application of this interpretation and the discriminatory effect it has on Italian citizens resident abroad comply with the principles of the TFEU?
Does it intend to launch an infringement procedure or other form of mediation against Italy to protect the rights of the EU citizens affected?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.9.2025) The Commission is aware of the matter raised by the Honourable Members and notes that it pertains to an issue of national competence to be addressed by national authorities and courts. Direct taxation falls essentially within the competence of Member States.

As confirmed by the Court of Justice of the European Union (hereinafter, ‘the Court’), in the absence of any harmonisation at EU level, Member States have retained the power to define, even unilaterally, the criteria for allocating their powers of taxation1.

The Court has also held that the criterion of nationality for the purpose of allocating fiscal jurisdiction between states which conclude bilateral tax treaties cannot be regarded as constituting any discrimination prohibited under the EU Treaties2. Hence, Article 1(2) of the Convention between Italy and Bulgaria does not appear to contravene EU law.

Since the application by Italy of the Convention concerned is not governed by EU law, the Commission is not competent to assess its compatibility with general principles of law such as legal certainty and legitimate expectations3.
Whether the changed interpretation or application of the 1988 Convention between Italy and Bulgaria would pose a legal problem is for the Member States concerned and their national courts to address.
1 van Hilten (C-513/03), paragraph 47. 2 Gilly (C-336/96), paragraph 30. 3 See, in particular, Society for the Protection of Unborn Children Ireland (C-159/90), paragraph 31; Friedrich

Kremzow (C-299/95), paragraph 15; Kühn (C-177/90), paragraph 14; Duff and Others (C-63/93), paragraph 20; Rombi and Arkopharma (C-107/97), paragraph 67; Weidacher (C-179/00), paragraph 31; Willy Gerekens and Association agricole pour la promotion de la commercialisation laitière Procola (C-459/02), paragraph 29.
